title: The last ten nights
hook: Somewhere in the next ten nights is one night better than a thousand months. Here's how to look for it.

screens.text: **Twenty days down.** Whether this is your first Ramadan or you've been Muslim for months, the best part is now. Hidden in the next ten nights is one night worth more than a lifetime.
**Laylat al-Qadr** (the Night of Decree) is the night the Qur'an was first sent down. The Qur'an says it's better than a thousand months [Q 97:1–5].
bubbles: Angels, with **Jibril** (Gabriel), come down, and it's peace until dawn [Q 97:1–5].

options.feedback: Yes. More than a whole lifetime of worship, in one night.
Not quite. A thousand months is over 83 years. One night is worth more than a lifetime.
Not quite. It's over 83 years: more than a lifetime, in one night.

screens.text: No one knows for sure. Drag to the end of the month: the Prophet ﷺ told us to look for it in the odd nights of the last ten, the 21st, 23rd, 25th, 27th and 29th [Bukhari 2017].

In these ten nights the Prophet ﷺ worked harder than at any other time, and woke his family to pray [Bukhari 2024]. Whoever prays on that night with faith, hoping for Allah's reward, has their past sins forgiven [Bukhari 1901].
bubbles: Islamic nights begin at sunset, so the 21st night is the evening before the 21st day.

screens.prompt: Does it count as "seeking" Laylat al-Qadr?

items.text: Praying Isha and two extra rak'ahs, then making du'a
items.why: Prayer and du'a are the heart of it.

items.text: Giving a few dollars in charity each of the ten nights
items.why: Many people give a little every night, so one gift lands on the Night of Decree.

items.text: Only staying up all night at the masjid; nothing else counts
items.why: The masjid is lovely, but worship at home counts too. Do what you can keep up.

items.text: Saying dhikr (remembering Allah) on your way home from work
items.why: Remembering Allah anywhere counts, and it's open to everyone.{women} That includes when you're on your period.{/women}

screens.text: **The night's du'a.** 'A'isha asked the Prophet ﷺ what to say if she knew it was the Night of Decree. He taught her a short du'a (prayer of asking) asking Allah for pardon [Tirmidhi 3513]. It's yours next.

screens.arabic: اللَّهُمَّ إِنَّكَ عَفُوٌّ كَرِيمٌ تُحِبُّ الْعَفْوَ فَاعْفُ عَنِّي
screens.meaning: O Allah, You are Pardoning and Generous, You love to pardon, so pardon me
screens.when: Any night of the last ten, especially the odd nights. Say it as often as you like. [Tirmidhi 3513]

screens.text: Say it a few times, one tap each. There's no set number: on these nights, say it as often as you like.

phrases.meaning: O Allah, You are Pardoning and Generous, You love to pardon, so pardon me

screens.situation: Hannah heard that Laylat al-Qadr is "definitely the 27th." She's tired, so she plans to rest the other nights and go all-out on the 27th only.

options.text: Do something small every odd night, and a bit more on the 27th
options.feedback: Yes. Many hope for the 27th, but the Prophet ﷺ said to seek it across the odd nights [Bukhari 2017].

options.text: Only the 27th; the rest don't matter
options.feedback: Not quite. No one knows the night for sure. A little each odd night covers them all.

options.text: Skip it; she can't do all ten nights perfectly
options.feedback: Not quite. Small and steady is enough. Even a short du'a each night is real worship.

screens.text: **I'tikaf** is staying in the masjid for worship. The Prophet ﷺ did it in the last ten days every year [Bukhari 2026]. Some masjids hold it, for all ten days or for one night. Ask {{masjid.name}}.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Laylat al-Qadr: the Qur'an was revealed in it; better than a thousand months; angels and the Spirit descend; peace until dawn [Q 97:1–5].
- Seek it in the odd nights of the last ten [Bukhari 2017]. The Prophet ﷺ strove hardest in the last ten and woke his family [Bukhari 2024]; he made i'tikaf in the last ten every year [Bukhari 2026].
- Praying on Laylat al-Qadr with faith and hope of reward forgives past sins [Bukhari 1901].
- The du'a taught to 'A'isha: *Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun karimun tuhibbul-'afwa fa'fu 'anni* [Tirmidhi 3513; sahih per al-Albani; the word *karim* appears in this narration's Arabic].
- A woman on her period can't pray or (in the Hanafi school) recite the Qur'an, but du'a, dhikr, charity and listening to the Qur'an are open to her all night.

**Likely questions**
- *"What should I ask for?"* Anything good: forgiveness, guidance for themselves and their family, a Muslim community, help with a struggle. Du'a for non-Muslim family's guidance is good. Any language.
- *"On my period?"* Yes: du'a, dhikr, charity, listening. The reward of the night isn't closed to her.
- *"I'tikaf?"* Staying in the masjid for worship; the masjid sets the rules (men usually in the main hall; arrangements for women vary). Short stays are fine for beginners. Hanafi details (the ten-day sunnah i'tikaf for men; women's i'tikaf at home in the Hanafi school) go to the imam.
- *"Signs?"* Some narrations describe a calm, mild night and a soft sunrise. Keep it light; signs aren't needed to benefit.
- *"Is it the 27th?"* Many scholars and communities hope for the 27th; the Prophet ﷺ said to seek the odd nights. Encourage all of them.

**Escalate:** detailed i'tikaf rulings; worship questions tied to a woman's own cycle beyond the basics.

**Don't**
- Don't state the 27th as certain.
- Don't make anyone feel their worship is worthless if they can't stay up.
